characters: Ewurama: a 10-year-old girl with neat braids, a red T-shirt and shorts, carrying a small notebook and pencil.
Issah: Ewurama’s friend, 10, in a blue shirt and cap, with a ruler in his pocket.
Maa Gifty: Ewurama’s aunt, a tomato seller in a yellow apron and head tie, at a market stall.

narrationPlan.voice: Bright, curious voice; Maa Gifty is warm and practical
narrationPlan.pace: Clear and curious, with a detective’s tone (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light plucked guitar with a quiet marketplace ambience (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Tomatoes are central to many Ghanaian dishes and markets; post-harvest loss is a real concern for traders, but this story deals with a small classroom-scale fair test only.

teacherGuide.overview: A fair-test story where children, not an expert, design and repeat the experiment. The honest ending models scientific humility.
learningGoals: Describe what makes a test fair (same size, same type, only one change).
Explain why repeating a test matters.
Record observations with dates, drawings and words.
beforeReading: Ask: why do some fruit and vegetables go bad faster than others?
whileReading: Pause at page 3 and let children name what must stay the same.
afterReading: Plan and run a class fair test using a safe, inexpensive item.
discussion: What was the one thing the friends changed?
Why did Ewurama say they had not tested everything?
reflection: Which question in your own home or school could you test?

mathsExtension.task: Maa Gifty lost 10 tomatoes out of 100. What percentage did she lose?
After the change, she lost 4 out of 100. How many fewer tomatoes did she lose?
Each plate held 3 tomatoes and there were 2 plates. How many tomatoes were in the first test?

support: Provide a table already drawn: Day, Sun plate, Shade plate.
stretch: Design a test for the damp cloth idea: what will you change, what must stay the same, and how will you measure it?

culturalNotes: Tomatoes are central to many Ghanaian dishes and markets; post-harvest loss is a real concern for traders, but this story deals with a small classroom-scale fair test only.
localiseThis: Use produce that is common in your area; the numbers in the maths tasks are made up.
Check the school’s rules for classroom experiments.

investigation.title: Sun or shade?
materials: 6 firm tomatoes of the same size (or another fruit)
steps: Choose one question and say what will change and what will stay the same.
Put 3 on a plate in the sun and 3 on a plate in the shade.
Look, touch gently and draw each day for 5 days.
Share your results and what you still do not know.
investigation.whatToNotice: Which changes appear first (wrinkling, soft patches, mould)? Are the results the same each time?
investigation.safetyNote: Never eat the tomatoes from the test. Wash hands after handling them and throw spoiled fruit away safely.
